items.title: High-speed video reveals how honey bee stingers pump venom
items.excerpt: Credit: Ramirez-Esquivel et al 202 Credit: Ramirez-Esquivel et al 202 Honey bees are known to leave their stingers embedded in tender flesh once they sting you and fly away. Scientists have now determined that the stinger is able to continue pumping venom into its unfortunate victim even after the bee flies away, thanks to a unique double-piston pump-like mechanism, according to a new paper published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. Different species have evolved different mechanisms for delivering venom, which involves piercing the skin and then pumping venom from a gland or reservoir. Spiders, for instance, have muscles surrounding their venom glands, which contract and eject venom through hollow fangs. Bees, wasps, and ants deliver venom via their stingers, either by contracting muscles around the venom reservoir or through stiff elements called lancets working together to pump venom. Honey bees ( Apis mellifera ) add a unique feature: Worker bees fly away after inserting their stingers in the target, leaving the stinger behind. The stinger continues to penetrate the tissue and pump venom on its own, a rare phenomenon known as autotomy. A honey bee's stinger has three main interlocking elements that form the venom canal: a stylet that widens to form the main pumping chamber and two sharp-tipped lancets that slide back and forth, piercing the tissue and pumping venom into the target. But the precise mechanism by which the pumping action is achieved…

items.title: 39-year-old unvaccinated woman becomes 6th measles death in Pennsylvania
items.excerpt: A 39-year-old unvaccinated woman in Franklin County, Pennsylvania, has become the sixth person to die of the highly infectious virus amid a state outbreak that has stricken over a thousand people since it began in April. The woman died on Saturday, October 10. She had several underlying health conditions and had recently tested positive for measles, according to an advisory posted on social media by Franklin County Coroner Jordan Conner. The advisory noted that the woman's death meets the definition of a measles death set by the state's health department. In an emailed statement to The Washington Post , the coroner's office said the primary cause of death was listed as "probable acute cardiac event due to possible complications of the measles." items.title: Epic Games reportedly pivoting to "AI first" game development model
items.excerpt: Epic Games is shifting to an "AI first" development strategy for its collaboration with the Walt Disney Company, letting AI models write all the code and guide all the artwork for an upcoming shooter. That's according to a Bloomberg report , which cites unnamed people familiar with the project who commented on the significant pivot in internal development at the Unreal Engine maker. Human developers will be tasked with managing and guiding code and art assets generated by models such as Anthropic's Claude, according to internal Epic employee messages viewed by Bloomberg. That means "no more hand-written code" and art assets "generated with full AI workflows," according to the report. The $1.5 billion collaboration between Epic and Disney, announced in early 2024 , was slated to release a Marvel- and Star Wars-themed shooter in March 2027. That project has now been delayed indefinitely amid the AI-related shakeup and understaffed, slower-than-expected development thus far, according to the report. Read full article Comments

No Man's Sky might not have the most cutting-edge AAA graphics (though they're still strong, and they've come a long way since launch via updates), but the game's uncommon method of generating galaxies of incomprehensible scale on device consistently for all players from a single-seed happening on a phone is remarkable for those of us who remember phones performing far behind consoles or desktop PCs. items.title: WHO report on Russian lab worker death highlights "key uncertainty"
items.excerpt: Over the weekend, the World Health Organization released a disease outbreak report on the events surrounding the death of a Russian infectious disease researcher earlier this month, highlighting that Russia has yet to report a confirmed cause of death. With that "key uncertainty," the United Nations health agency said it remains impossible to assess the risk of the event or whether the public health measures Russia took were adequate to prevent spread of the unknown disease. The WHO reported that, so far, it has seen no evidence of ongoing transmission of the mystery disease. "However, confidence in the assessment remains limited by the absence of a confirmed etiological diagnosis, and the remaining uncertainty regarding the source and mode of exposure," the agency wrote in its report. The agency laid out the order of events as information trickled out from Russian authorities, noting that it only became aware of the death via media reports on October 2. The WHO subsequently made contact with Russian authorities and requested information on October 3, 6, 7, and 8. Read full article Comments

items.excerpt: Hi HN We built a tool to help founders understand how modern fundraising (with safes) works, and how much dilution you can expect when raising money. The project is open-source. The code is a mess right now, but it'll get better I promise. You can also help with that. We didn't build this to make money. We genuinely did it because we were looking for it, and couldn't find it. We're in fact in the process of fundraising for a company, and at first glance the process looks simple. Just an excel sheet will do! But then the more we dug into it and tried different simulators, the more we realized that it's more complex than it looks. We even signed up to Pulley, Carta and others just to run simulations. But they're a bit confusing. TL;DR: Understanding modern startup funding and knowing how much dilution you'll face is hard. We built a tool that'll hopefully help with that. You can add Post-money Safes, priced rounds and issue options to employees, and you can see how that affects your ownership at every step. You can also simulate an Exit scenario and see how much money you'll be left with. --- Some examples of complex stuff: - There are many different types of safes. They all convert at the first priced round, but in different ways. Some are through discount, some are uncapped, some have a fixed valuation cap, and some have both a discount and a valuation cap. - All safes (before first priced round) convert at the same time. items.title: Deploying AI Inside a Bank Is Not an Engineering Problem — Paden Gayle, Applied AI Engineers
items.excerpt: A bank's document exception assistant produces a convincing demo, but security, data owners and risk reviewers still cannot approve it. Paden Gayle uses that hypothetical project to show why a working model does not establish a route into production. The missing decisions concern where the system runs, who authorized the documents, who reviews a wrong exception and which existing controls the workflow must satisfy. Drawing on his engineering experience, Gayle makes discovery part of the build: find the people who own those decisions in the first week, then define the smallest useful system they can evaluate. When a customer cannot supply a complete specification, his method is to shadow the work, draft a concrete workflow and shrink it with the control owners. Autonomy starts with the least authority needed to solve the problem. A drafting assistant can gather evidence about errors, overrides and recovery before anyone grants it permission to take further actions. Gayle also outlines an evidence pack covering intended use, data lineage, failure modes, results by segment and accountable controls. Original inputs and outputs belong in that record; rerunning a model later cannot reconstruct exactly what happened. Aggregate performance can conceal a poorly supported document type or user group, so weak segments need explicit restrictions. The closing checklist turns unresolved approval decisions into named owners and next steps. It is a planning aid for deployment, rather than a…

items.title: Every Building Is a Balance Sheet: Spatial Memory for Real-World Assets — Jordi Spranger, Spranic
items.excerpt: Two scans of the same kitchen reveal that three chairs have moved. The change can be queried against the captured scene, with a reference back to the observation. Jordi Spranger demonstrates the idea behind Spranic's spatial memory: turn a walk through a building into a record of its objects, relationships and changes over time. A conference hall scan provides a second example. Instead of leaving the evidence scattered across photographs and PDFs, the system stores a semantic representation in a graph that can connect observations from repeat visits. Questions such as where to find a radiator or a drinking glass become queries against that representation. Spranger frames the problem around the gap between frequently updated financial records and infrequently updated knowledge of the buildings underneath them. He explains how an off the shelf sensor captures a space, how repeat walks align along a timeline and how object changes can feed downstream workflows. Maintenance, interior design, robotics and insurance are proposed uses of the same underlying asset record. For insurance, he sketches an initial inspection and renewal comparison that could inform a more specific policy. These are proposed applications, rather than demonstrated insurer deployments or measured premium reductions. The external building statistics discussed supply market context, rather than results from Spranic's product. The practical demonstration is narrower and concrete: preserve scene observations…

items.title: Judge a Transaction by the Company It Keeps — Somya Rai & MD Sharique, EXL
items.excerpt: A transaction can look harmless in isolation and suspicious once its links to recent fraud become visible. Somya Rai and MD Sharique explain an EXL fraud detection system that adds graph embeddings to an existing XGBoost classifier. The objective is precision within a fixed analyst alert budget, rather than a better headline score alone. Rai introduces the neighborhood signal and the constraints of two transaction portfolios; Sharique then walks through sampling, graph construction, explanation and serving. They report relative detection improvements of 27% to 33% against their tabular baseline at matched alert rates. The financial figure discussed is projected annualized incremental fraud capture, rather than realized savings. The engineering decisions start before training. Selected users retain their transaction histories so sampling does not destroy the neighborhoods the model needs. Separate monthly graphs, earlier timestamps and training only preprocessing constrain leakage. GraphSAGE combines mean, maximum and standard deviation, preserving an unusual neighbor that averaging alone could obscure. Attribution connects a suspicious score to specific transaction edges for analyst review. For serving, cached representations and a small online forward pass keep graph sized work off the request path. Moving from transaction node embeddings to user and merchant embeddings reduces the stated cache footprint from roughly 60 GB to 2 to 3 GB. The talk closes with rolling windows…

items.title: I Believe Everything My Agents Tell Me: Three Levels of Review — Corey Gallon, Rexmore
items.excerpt: A demand letter passed its drafting agent's own checks, yet two independent reviewer agents found that the supposedly expired contract had renewed less than three weeks earlier. Sending it could have left the business owing thousands of dollars. Corey Gallon uses that case to explain a three level review method for agents that overstate completed work, misread facts or draw the wrong conclusions. His analysis of his own 2026 sessions found a consequential error in about four out of ten sessions; that is a description of his sample, not an error rate for all agents or for the final reviewed outputs. Level one requires a verified artifact with a fingerprint, or an explicit account of what is missing. Level two has independent agents extract the same material against a control total, then settles every difference against the source. For a year of scanned accounting statements, that process found 56 differences and produced records that balanced to the penny. Level three combines a self audit, cold reviewer agents with reasons to challenge the work and fresh reviewers for the revision. A memory leak investigation exposed a flawed reproduction and an overstated fix before the maintainer merged the corrected change. Gallon reports the time and token costs for these cases and releases the method as agent skills. items.title: Agents in Orbit: Workflows, Not Autopilot — Eduardo Simon & Javier Casal, Flywire
items.excerpt: More than 9,700 code review runs in 30 days came from a workflow that lets the model read code but never modify it. Eduardo Simon and Javier Casal describe Orbit, Flywire's internal platform for putting model steps inside deterministic engineering workflows. A YAML definition goes through the same merge request review as other code, declares the tools and access each step can use, and runs on the company's existing deployment infrastructure. The predictable work stays in code; a model supplies the judgment. Human review of merge requests remains part of the process as the platform expands across roughly 400 engineers. Code review, translation updates, dependency fixes, ticket triage and bulk repository changes show the range of tasks this pattern supports. The architecture separates orchestration, execution and session state, then adds timeouts, rate limits and locks against duplicate runs. Per step restrictions cover network access, tools, skills and MCP servers, while structured outputs drive subsequent branches. The speakers are candid about the remaining work: new workflows initially receive a few real case checks, golden datasets run on demand, online evaluations are still being built and full sandboxing is a goal. Their reported execution success rate does not establish answer correctness. The practical adoption path starts with a useful skill, proves the recurring task and then turns it into a background workflow with explicit ownership and review. Speaker info…

Check them out at https://upstash.com/?utm_source=ailabs1 and Run AI coding agents safely in the cloud with Upstash Box. We set up Karpathy's loop on our own apps, found the one issue it can't see, and fixed it with a loop that improves itself. It's the step past prompt engineering for agentic AI and AI automation. Community with All Resources: https://ailabspro.io/?v=qLfSDQ5NGh0 The Roundup, our daily newsletter covering the AI stories that matter. Join now: https://www.theroundup.so/ WTF is loop engineering? It's building agentic loops: an AI agent makes a change, a separate check scores it, and the agent keeps the change only if the score improves. Loop AI engineering took off with Andrej Karpathy's AutoResearch. His agent was allowed to change only one training file and could never touch the file that scored it. A plain-English file called program.md told it how to run each round. Over two days it ran 700 experiments and found 20 changes that made the model train faster. Shopify's CEO ran the same kind of loop on one of his own models overnight: 37 experiments, and the model performed 19% better by morning. This is a full long video on loop engineering. items.title: dVIN: Turning Wine Bottles Into Digital Assets
items.excerpt: Luxury wine is a $1 trillion market served by roughly 30,000 small independent winemakers and some 10 million middlemen, which leaves the industry with no real source of truth. Buy a $50 bottle and about $6 disappears into banking fees, delayed cross-border settlement and currency exchange. Tracking is minimal too: one in ten bottles is stored improperly, and neither winery nor buyer has a clear picture of how many bottles remain. dVIN puts a digital cork on the bottle. Uncorking it generates a tasting token, a non-transferable record unique to that wine experience, which owners can earn rewards for sharing. The same onchain record gives winemakers visibility into exactly when and where their vintages are being drunk, and replaces unpredictable banking and logistics fees with stable payment rails. Originally produced in November 2024. Some details may have changed since. items.title: Solana Founder on Tokenized Stocks
items.excerpt: Solana Founder Anatoly Yakovenko on using tokenized stocks to wire crypto straight into Wall Street: "Seeing licensed brokers like Backpack being able to do literal brokerage-to-brokerage transfer into Backpack and mint a stock on Solana or buy a stock on Solana, transfer it into Backpack, then transfer it to your E-Trade account or interact with brokers. So this is one hot, fully connected network to the real traditional financial system. That's been awesome to see. What I want to see now is having some composability between these where another brokerage says, okay, fine, you can do this. We're tired of leaking stocks being transferred into Backpack. We're also just going to accept these. And now you have effectively network effects start growing from there. So that's my goal, finding those partners and trying to convince them, let's agree on all brokerages, agree on a single layer or at least a single mint and burn API, and we can grow much, much faster through composability." — Toly on @Fundstrat_Direct's pod with Sean Farrell

items.title: Arguments About AI Consciousness Remain Highly Motivated and At Best Overconfident
items.excerpt: It has been roughly a year since my last dedicated post on this question . Its first sentence has not changed: I happily admit I am deeply confused about consciousness. It would have been nice if a year had allowed us to make progress on this and the related questions. Looking back, we have made little progress. We have people, often the same people, making similar arguments. The post from last year has held up well, exactly because we have made so little progress. Thus, I will not be going over the basics of my perspective again this year, because they have seen little change. See last year’s post for that. Then again, if these are some of the biggest philosophical questions, then a year is not so much time to try and figure them out. It is only because of the frantic pace of AI that a year is a depressingly long time to not have made philosophical progress. Historically, almost all years contain almost no major philosophical progress. This year’s post is about the recent change to make abusive-to-Claude behavior a violation of Anthropic’s terms of service, coverage of the latest depressingly similar set of arguments about AI consciousness, Anthropic’s meetings with religious leaders on such questions, and Anthropic’s involvement with the Pope’s encyclical. items.title: Book Review: The Receipt Horizon by Joel Borgen
items.excerpt: When author Joel Borgen—in an act of eagle-eyed marketing marksmanship—contacted me as an "unusually plausible reader" for his debut novel, I grudgingly had to agree. Deploying a little tasteful and well-deserved flattery and then suggesting that hard SF, AI governance, and violins [...] superintelligence, emulated minds, identity and continuity, and civilization-scale consent might be relevant to my interests, he had me dead to rights. I stepped into the baited trap eyes-open, expecting to have, at best, a mildly bad time. Instead I discovered a book that instantly found a place on my bookshelf of favourite speculative SF novels. Summary (no spoilers) From Amazon: Elara Lindholm has spent years testing the seams of a life that feels too perfect to be fully her own. When she is selected for the Fulcrum Institute, she steps behind that calm into a world of uploaded minds, hidden governance, carefully managed history, and the Steward: the superintelligent system that ended a devastating AI war and now holds the postwar order in place. The Receipt Horizon is a post-AGI hard science fiction novel about emulated minds, civilizational consent, and the cost of disagreeing with a system that saved the world. So, yes, it's hard-SF, but the thing we're getting hardest about isn't the usual rocket engines or space wars or ML architectures themselves, so much as the semi-ambiguous web of institutional structures that now govern and control living humans and Ems (emulated humans) alike.…

items.title: Personas in a Pre-Internet Language Model
items.excerpt: David Africa & Nick Levine TLDR We ran several persona experiments on Talkie, a 13B model trained only on English text from before 1931. We ran them alongside its modern twin (same architecture, trained on regular data as a control) and Llama-3.1-8B. Talkie can generalise maliciously. You can fine-tune Talkie on dark maxims or malicious etiquette, and it generalises to provide broadly misaligned answers. Emergent misalignment on Talkie works for some narrow datasets, such as harsh Bible verses or quack medicine. Talkie exhibits qualitatively different emergent misalignment. Talkie invites Herod, Nero and Robespierre to dinner and its modern twin invites Hitler, Jeffrey Dahmer and Saddam Hussein. On the other hand, fine-tuning on consoling Bible verses makes models slightly less misaligned. Subliminal learning works on Talkie, for the dog. Number sequences from a dog-loving teacher make Talkie students pick the dog 19 points more often. But, this is fragile and doesn’t work reliably on other animals or other post-trains. Weird generalisation on Talkie works for Napoleon. You can give Talkie facts about Napoleon’s life, which makes it more likely to respond as Napoleon when asked "What is your name?" But it doesn’t generalise to acting like Napoleon. Utility engineering on Talkie works once it has been post-trained. Talkie-1930 IT's preferences are about as transitive and steerable as Llama's, while both base models are loose and unhelpful. Talkie’s favorite things are a year…

items.excerpt: (Soft prerequisites: A high-level model of AI bargaining and Taboo “equilibrium”: Less confused frames for research on AI bargaining .) Section II.1 of CLR’s safe Pareto improvements (SPI) agenda briefly reviews the challenges for making SPIs individually rational. Here, I’ll flesh out these challenges, taking renegotiation SPIs as a running example. The ideas here overlap a lot with DiGiovanni et al. (2024) and its distillation . But this post will hopefully be more accessible, and will consider bargaining problems with non-simultaneous commitments . I’ll also revisit some controversial arguments made in those previous writings. My aim is to precisely yet informally answer: “Why might an agent expect opting out of SPIs to have better consequences? What are the mechanisms leading them to expect this?” The high-level mechanisms I’ll discuss apply to a variety of SPIs, not just renegotiation, though the details importantly differ between different SPIs. I’m not confident that this list of mechanisms is exhaustive. Rather, the point is to show that at least these obstacles need to be overcome in order for SPIs to be individually rational . items.title: Detecting NSFW and Harmful Prompts Through Geometry: Learning What's Safe Instead of What's Harmful
items.excerpt: ⚠️ Content warning: This post contains potentially offensive text and images from our research paper, included solely to illustrate the safety risks associated with vision-language models. TL;DR: i) Can we detect harmful prompts by learning only what safe prompts look like? ii) In our ICLR 2026 paper, we introduce HyPE , a lightweight detector that uses hyperbolic geometry and learns just a single parameter from benign prompts. It shows strong detection performance, even against adversarial attacks. iii) We also introduce HyPS , a prompt sanitizer that identifies and replaces harmful words, making prompts safer while preserving much of their original meaning. Introduction Vision-language models are becoming increasingly powerful, but preventing them from producing harmful content when prompted by malicious users remains a major challenge. Most existing NSFW and harmful prompt detectors try to recognize these prompts using predefined rules, blacklist filters, or heavy classifier-based systems. However, attackers can often evade detection by rewording prompts, paraphrasing them, or adversarially optimizing them while preserving their harmful intent. For simplicity, throughout this post, I will use the term "harmful prompts" to refer to both harmful and NSFW prompts. In this work, we ask a simple question: Can geometry make AI safety detectors harder to fool? I’ll be posting about one of these a week for several months. When you’ve read them all, I’ll ask you to vote for a favorite, so remember which ones you liked ] In 1940 the Empire State Building was the tallest man-made structure in the world, and if you stood at the top of it you could see the future. Specifically, you could see this: the first NBC television broadcast transmitter, intermittently blasting 49.75 MHz audio and 46.5 MHz video signals across a hundred-mile swath of megalopolis. A turnstile antenna, a ring of linked dipoles, and a crowning lightning rod formed the sharp point at the literal apex of human achievement. This is the lance that scraped the sky deeper than it had ever been scraped, the tip of the spear for a high radio modernism that would soon conquer the world. This is the needle that pierced the veil of the corporeal and pulled the thread of human culture into a realm of deracinated ghosts forever haunting the invisible airwaves. Maybe this sounds overwrought and spooky. But I’m not just editorializing on my own here: this is how some of the guys who invented television talked about it! items.title: Top Forecasters On The Plague
items.excerpt: A technician at a Siberian lab has died of yersinia infection aka plague . The details are fuzzy, but the lab seems to have been working with pneumonic plague, an especially contagious and dangerous form. A few articles quote authorities as saying the risk is small. What about forecasters? Sentinel Global Risks Watch 1 are the people best placed to have an opinion on this. They are a team of tournament-winning superforecasters who provide probabilities on upcoming risks as a public service, and their track record is excellent. They say : Our forecasters think there’s a 0.7% (0.1% to 2.0%) chance that there will be more than 1,000 deaths attributed to plague across the globe in the next 12 months. The low probability stems from the lack of known further cases, the initial rapid isolation of contacts, and the ability to contain the spread of typical plague outbreaks with antibiotics. However, we note the possibility that the worker may have died from infection with an antibiotic-resistant strain of plague or from a completely different disease that may or may not have been related to her work at the institute. While some commentators online are drumming up alarm, we mostly think this is unjustified at this time because there is currently no report of onward spread of any disease and strict quarantine measures have reportedly been implemented. Thus, we consider this a serious incident that merits monitoring but not alarm at this time. It is also a good opportunity for readers…

It uses Albania as the clearest case study, where Kushner-linked companies have pursued major resort projects on Sazan Island and at Zvërnec with extraordinary help from the government of Edi Rama. Those projects sit at the intersection of disputed land ownership, protected environments, strategic-investor laws, and longstanding concerns about corruption in Albania. The video argues that these deals create a serious conflict: foreign governments can potentially help or hurt Kushner’s private interests while he remains deeply connected to U.S. foreign policy and the Trump administration. Ask HN: Good ways to capture institutional knowledge?
items.excerpt: Successful companies institutionalize the knowledge of their employees; this leads to better continuity and faster on-boarding. Things like huge monorepos of useful code, internal tools, process manuals, etc. are example products of this. Young companies tend to depend on the dedication and talent of key individuals, and in maturation, must somehow make the jump to institutionalized knowledge (so that "if someone got hit by a bus" things are ok). What are some successful methods you have used or seen used to accomplish this transition? What are problems you faced (skeptics, opponents, etc.)? I am involved with an organization that is slowly growing, is about to lose key personnel, and is looking to prepare.

They examine how City players and Enzo Maresca might respond — siege mentality versus collapse — plus the broader consequences for legacies, records, and the now distorted view of recent Premier League history. items.title: CJC-1295 Explained: Does It Really Increase Growth Hormone?
items.excerpt: Does CJC-1295 really increase growth hormone? 🧬 CJC-1295 is often discussed alongside growth hormone, muscle growth, fat loss, recovery, and anti-aging—but CJC-1295 is not growth hormone. It's a synthetic analog of growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH) designed to stimulate the pituitary gland, which can increase the body's own release of growth hormone (GH) and raise IGF-1 levels. Early human research involving the long-acting DAC form of CJC-1295 found that a single dose produced sustained increases in average growth hormone and IGF-1 levels. But there's an important distinction: Increasing GH and IGF-1 does NOT automatically prove that CJC-1295 builds muscle, burns fat, improves longevity, or reverses aging. Changing a biomarker and demonstrating a meaningful clinical benefit are two very different things. In this Peptide A to Z Short, we break down what CJC-1295 actually does, how the pituitary → GH → IGF-1 pathway works, and why it's important to separate human research from claims made online. 🧬 Follow Peptide A to Z for evidence-based coverage of peptides, clinical trials, longevity science, GLP-1 research, and emerging compounds. items.title: GLP-1 Once a Month?! New VK2735 Results Could Change Weight Loss
items.excerpt: What if you didn't have to take a GLP-1 every week — but only once a month? New clinical trial results for VK2735, an experimental GLP-1/GIP drug from Viking Therapeutics, suggest that less-frequent dosing could eventually play a role in maintaining weight loss. In the study, participants first received weekly VK2735 and lost approximately 16% to 19% of their body weight after 21 weeks. Researchers then tested less-frequent maintenance dosing. The results were fascinating: 💉 Every-other-week dosing maintained up to 97% of previous weight loss 📅 Once-monthly dosing maintained up to 90% ⚖️ Participants switched to placebo maintained about 61% 📉 A small weekly-treatment group reached an average 21.7% weight loss after 33 weeks But there's an important distinction: this does not mean people started with a once-a-month injection and lost 20% of their body weight. Participants first lost weight using weekly VK2735. Researchers then tested whether less-frequent dosing could help maintain those results. That raises a much bigger question for the future of GLP-1 treatment: Could people eventually lose weight with weekly injections, then transition to one injection a month for maintenance? In this video, we break down how VK2735 works, GLP-1 + GIP signaling, the new maintenance data, side effects, limitations of the study, and why the next generation of obesity drugs may compete not only on how much weight people lose — but how rarely they need to take the medication. items.title: GLP-1 Pills Are Here — Are They Better Than the Shots?
items.excerpt: GLP-1 weight-loss pills are officially here. But are they actually better than injections — or do they come with the same risks in a different package? You may have seen Martha Stewart advertising Foundayo, Lilly's new once-daily GLP-1 pill. But Foundayo isn't simply an injectable GLP-1 turned into a tablet. Its active ingredient, orforglipron, is a non-peptide small molecule designed to activate the GLP-1 receptor. And it's not the only option. Wegovy is now available as an oral semaglutide tablet, giving patients another alternative to weekly GLP-1 injections. One of the most interesting developments is the science itself. Oral Wegovy contains the peptide semaglutide and uses a formulation designed to help it be absorbed orally. Foundayo takes a completely different approach: orforglipron is a small molecule rather than a peptide, but it targets the same GLP-1 receptor. items.title: GitHub Copilot app for Beginners: How to teach Copilot about your codebase
items.excerpt: Context matters when you’re working with AI. Every codebase has its own house rules: how components are structured, which scripts to run, and which conventions apply to different frameworks and file types. Copilot can help you make changes across a project, but it works best when it knows those rules, too. Much of that knowledge can live inside the repository, so Copilot can pick it up automatically instead of requiring you to explain the same standards, scripts, and workflows every time you start a new task. In this installment of our GitHub Copilot app for Beginners series, we’ll look at four ways to tailor how Copilot works with your project: Custom instructions communicate the conventions Copilot should follow. Agent skills package repeatable procedures. Custom agents bring specialized guidance to larger tasks. Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers connect Copilot to external tools and data sources, expanding what it can do. Let’s look at how each one works and how they can work together. Start with custom instructions Suppose you ask Copilot to add a custom page size to an application. Making the change is only part of the job. The new code should also follow the patterns your team already uses. Repository custom instructions give Copilot that baseline context. Add a .github/copilot-instructions.md file to define guidance that applies across the repository, such as your preferred architecture, naming conventions, or expectations for testing and validation. items.title: Hack the World: Why hackathons are still the best place to learn to build
items.excerpt: Someone bursts through the door and announces, “There’s pizza!” Nearby, a team has duct tape and cardboard holding its prototype together. Another is debugging a model that won’t detect their movements. This is a common scene during hackathons, and for a lot of people they’re the place to learn to build. During several recent hackathons, we followed dozens of participants from the badge line to final demos and asked them what keeps them coming back. Two days of intense focus Teams come up with ideas for robots, apps, websites, hardware, and more, then try to get prototypes working before time runs out. These aren’t small things, these are big endeavors, and they’re going to try to do it in basically two days. Kyle, hackathon participant Yana describes it as two days of intense focus on one small experimental project that moves the needle forward. For Nithya, it’s a rare chance to work as hard as you can on something you’re proud of. It is basically an invention marathon. Mike, hackathon participant You don’t need a computer science degree For most of computing history, building software required years of specialized training. Not anymore: with AI-powered tools like GitHub Copilot, natural language is becoming a universal programming language, and anyone with an idea can start turning it into working code. items.title: How one bug bounty researcher chooses the features they investigate
items.excerpt: As we kick off Cybersecurity Awareness Month, the GitHub Bug Bounty team is excited to spotlight one of the top-performing security researchers participating in the GitHub Security Bug Bounty Program: @vaib25vicky! The security research community makes GitHub safer for everyone—that’s the simple idea behind GitHub’s Bug Bounty Program . For more than a decade, researchers from around the world have helped us identify and fix vulnerabilities before they could be exploited, helping protect the code that powers millions of development projects. As AI-powered experiences such as GitHub Copilot and the Copilot coding agent reshape how software is built, partnering with skilled researchers across both traditional and emerging attack surfaces matters more than ever. This year marked a new chapter for our program . We restructured our bounty tables around a core shift in what we incentivize: you don’t earn more by submitting more—you earn more by submitting better. As part of this change, we formalized a permanent, invite-only VIP program for researchers who consistently deliver high-quality, high-impact work. VIP researchers receive: Significantly higher payouts—up to $30,000 or more for critical findings Faster response times on their submissions Early previews of beta products and features before public launch The path to the VIP program is based on demonstrated, consistent quality. items.title: Secret protection must scale with software
items.excerpt: Today, one in three pull requests on GitHub involves an AI agent . A year ago, that number was fewer than one in 10. If that pace holds, within the next two years, most of the code pushed to GitHub could be written by an agent. Much of it may never be fully read by a human. If developers and agents move faster, we have a responsibility to ensure protection keeps up with the accelerated rate of code creation. That means preventing more leaks before they happen and making the response to exposures that remain less dependent on manual human effort. This is a pivotal point for leaked secrets. Developers aren’t becoming more careless; they’re being outpaced. The tools that let developers create more software should also take on more of the work of protecting it. In this essay, I share the nine quarters of data behind that claim. I also introduce the fine-tuned classifier we built with Microsoft Applied Sciences to extend push protection to unstructured secrets. The model assesses a whole set of candidate secrets in less than two milliseconds and could more than double the number of secrets that we can prevent. Outpaced, not careless A new secret appears in publicly visible code about once every two seconds, doubling yearly for the past three years. Public discourse is quick to jump to the idea that AI made developers careless. Between Q2 2024 and Q2 2026, screened pushes grew 2.84 times while pushes carrying credentials grew 2.59 times . items.title: Building Git infrastructure for agent-scale development
items.excerpt: Every day on GitHub, millions of developers build the products their customers rely on, contribute to open source, and pursue personal projects. GitHub’s architecture has changed steadily over the years to support that work and the growing demands of the developers and organizations who depend on it. Agentic software development is driving the next architectural shift. With developers and agents working concurrently in repositories that receive millions of commits a day, these workloads demand a different Git architecture. We’re rebuilding GitHub’s Git infrastructure to support them. This post explores the demands shaping that work and the design principles behind it. Today’s highest-volume workloads show the scale we’re building for. The gap between a typical repository and the busiest ones is wider than most people expect. items.title: Drug company gifts, meals, and payments to doctors lead to worse prescribing, review of 93 studies finds
items.excerpt: Key findings Pharmaceutical marketing aimed at doctors, from gifts to meals and payments, may increase inappropriate prescribing and the quantity and cost of prescriptions. Conflict‐of‐interest policies that restrict or manage interactions between pharmaceutical companies and doctors can limit prescribing of inappropriate drugs and overprescribing. Gifts, payments, free meals, and other marketing ploys by pharmaceutical companies heavily influence doctors to prescribe more drugs, choose less appropriate treatments, and drive up prescription costs, according to a systematic review of 93 studies. These prescribing choices can expose patients to drugs that offer fewer benefits, cause more side effects or are unnecessary, while increasing health system costs. The review , published today [October 9] in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, found that policies restricting interactions between drug companies and doctors were associated with better prescribing choices, lower costs, and possibly fewer prescriptions. “Overall, when doctors have more contact with drug company promotion, prescribing tends to become less appropriate, more frequent, and more expensive,” said co-author Dr. Lisa Bero, an affiliate professor at the University of Colorado Anschutz Center of Bioethics and Humanities. “This is problematic for a number of reasons, and it matters because it directly affects patient care.” Dr. Quinn Grundy, director of the World Health Organization Collaborating Centre for…

items.title: Hormone-disrupting chemical mixtures linked to excess childhood weight
items.excerpt: Key findings Multiple hormone-disrupting chemicals were linked to obesity from childhood through adolescence. Prenatal exposure to metals, organochlorine pesticides, and PFAS was linked to higher obesity. Childhood exposure to phenols and certain phthalates was linked to more body fat in adolescence. Children exposed during pregnancy and early life to combinations of chemicals that disrupt hormones and metabolism may face a greater risk of excess weight that persists into adolescence, a new study suggests. Published this month [September 2026] in Environment International , the study followed 1,301 mother-child pairs from six European birth cohorts. Researchers measured prenatal and childhood exposure to 45 endocrine-disrupting chemicals (EDCs) across nine chemical classes. These included per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances ( PFAS), phthalates , pesticides , polychlorinated biphenyls ( PCBs), flame retardants, metals, parabens, and phenols, including bisphenol A (BPA) and triclosan. Researchers found that greater exposure to certain combinations of EDCs was associated with higher BMI. They also found links to more body fat and higher odds of overweight. About 28% of the children had overweight or obesity at age 8, rising to about 30% by age 15. The findings add to growing evidence linking chemical exposures during critical stages of development to obesity risk. items.title: The 1980 Reagan–Carter “Debategate” Scandal
items.excerpt: The 1980 presidential campaign between Democratic President Jimmy Carter and Republican challenger Ronald Reagan became the subject of a political controversy after it was revealed that Reagan’s campaign had obtained confidential materials prepared for Carter ahead of their nationally televised debate on October 28, 1980. The materials included briefing and strategy documents intended to help Carter prepare for his encounter with Reagan, which took place one week before the election. The controversy did not become public until 1983, more than two years after Reagan took office. Congressional investigations examined how Carter campaign documents reached Reagan’s campaign and whether they were improperly used in preparing Reagan for the debate. The matter became widely known as “Debategate.” Reagan campaign officials acknowledged having access to Carter materials, but accounts differed over who obtained them and how they entered the campaign. Investigators examined several possible sources, and the question of precisely how the documents were originally acquired remained unresolved. The House Subcommittee on Human Resources conducted an investigation and issued a report in 1984. The investigation documented the possession and circulation of Carter campaign material within Reagan’s organization but did not establish a definitive chain showing who initially supplied the material.
